name: Paku Karen
sweep_summary: Paku Karen (paku1238, jkp) is not in the catalog. Both works with stress in the title are Glottolog artefacts: the reference pages for Giorgi 2016 (Italian epistemic adverbs, Benjamins, paywalled; Crossref abstract read) and Churng 2007 (American Sign Language topic/focus prosody, UWWPL 26, open PDF downloaded and read) each carry the note 'Paku Karen [jkp] (computerized assignment from \"phases\")' — an automatic title trigger from Luce 1985 'Phases of Pre-Pagan Burma'. Neither concerns Paku or word stress; priority none. The 137-reference Glottolog list for paku1238 in is very likely dominated by the same 'phases' trigger and should be treated as noise. As a by-product the author preprint of Kato 2021 'Typological profile of Karenic languages' (a works still to obtain from our earlier reading) was found open on Kato's Keio homepage and. it gives only a family-level statement (sesquisyllabic words: unstressed minor first syllable, stressed tone-bearing second syllable; 'Karenic languages generally have sesquisyllabic words') and names Paku only for consonants and negation. No Paku-specific stress statement was found.

earlier_scan.source_named: Only survey/minimal refs (Grierson LSI Burma 1920-29 listed by Glottolog as a minimal description; Luce 1985 wordlist; ISO change request) - no phonology or grammar of Paku Karen exists

new_statements.quote: EPK has many disyllabic words that have an atonal first syllable. These are "sesquisyllabic" in Matisoff's (1973: 84ff) terms, in that they are composed of the unstressed first syllable and the stressed second syllable. [...] SK also has many sesquisyllabic words, such as /kәsà/ 'lord, master', /kәshɔ́/ 'elephant', /θәrâ/ 'teacher', /tәkhwá/ 'cousin', /θәwɔ́/ 'village', /pәnà/ 'buffalo', and /lәpɔ́/ 'wave'. Karenic languages generally have sesquisyllabic words.
new_statements.citation: Kato, Atsuhiko (2021). Typological profile of Karenic languages. In Sidwell & Jenny (eds.), The Languages and Linguistics of Mainland Southeast Asia, 337-367. De Gruyter Mouton (author preprint).
new_statements.reading: CAVEAT: this is a family-level (Karenic) statement illustrated with Eastern Pwo and Sgaw Karen, not a first-hand statement about Paku Karen; Paku is only named elsewhere in the chapter (voiced stops, negation). Reading: Karenic words are tone-bearing monosyllables or sesquisyllables whose reduced first syllable is unstressed and whose final full syllable is stressed — i.e. prominence is on the full (tone-bearing) syllable, no contrastive positional word stress. No Paku-specific stress statement exists in any source opened in this or our earlier reading.
new_statements.found_by: works with stress in the title

sources.citation: Kato, Atsuhiko (2021). Typological profile of Karenic languages. In Paul Sidwell & Mathias Jenny (eds.), The Languages and Linguistics of Mainland Southeast Asia, 337-367. Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter Mouton. [author preprint, not a works with stress in the title; located via author homepage during this search of works with stress in the title]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: EPK has atonal syllables, which are phonetically unstressed and short, and cannot occur utterance-finally. [...] EPK has many disyllabic words that have an atonal first syllable. These are "sesquisyllabic" in Matisoff's (1973: 84ff) terms, in that they are composed of the unstressed first syllable and the stressed second syllable. [...] Karenic languages generally have sesquisyllabic words. [...] In PK and SK, the minor syllable in a sesquisyllabic word never has a tone; however, in some other Karenic languages, it may bear tones.
sources.locator: Preprint sect. 18.2.2 Suprasegmental phonemes, preprint p. 7 (extracted text page 7); Paku named on preprint p. 6
sources.note: Family-level only: Karenic words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic, with the minor (first) syllable unstressed and the full second syllable stressed and tone-bearing; examples are Eastern Pwo and Sgaw Karen, with Kayah Li and Kayan cited. Paku itself is named only for retaining Proto-Karen voiced stops with a four-way stop contrast (after Shintani 2003b) and for its verb-negation pattern; there is no Paku-specific stress statement. Read as a tone-language profile with stress = full-syllable vs. minor-syllable, not a positional word-stress rule.
